product: BLUETTI Elite 100 mini Portable Power Station (1,004.8 Wh, 700 W)

price_today.value: $429.00 at the BLUETTI US store (variant 49212162277595, in stock; compare-at $429.00, so no markdown)

wins.need: A 1 kWh battery that fits on a shelf, under a desk or in a car footwell
wins.claim: Takes the least floor space of the 1 kWh units checked, against BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 and Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2. Arithmetic from the makers' dimensions: the mini is 9.3 x 8.5 in = 79 sq in. The Elite 100 V2 is 12.6 x 8.5 in = 107 sq in, so the mini is 26% smaller. The Anker C1000 Gen 2 is 15.12 x 8.19 in = 124 sq in, so the mini is 36% smaller. The mini is also slightly lighter: 23.6 lb, against 25 lb (Elite 100 V2) and 24.9 lb (Anker).
wins.figure: 79 sq in footprint, 23.6 lb (rivals: 107 sq in and 25 lb; 124 sq in and 24.9 lb)
wins.who: BLUETTI and Anker US product pages; the arithmetic is ours

wins.need: The most stored energy for the money at about 1 kWh
wins.claim: Lowest price per rated Wh of the 1 kWh stations priced at maker stores today. Arithmetic: $429 / 1,004.8 Wh = $0.43/Wh. EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic is $459 / 1,024 Wh = $0.45/Wh. BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 is $499 / 1,024 Wh = $0.49/Wh.
wins.who: Store prices read with storecheck; the arithmetic is ours

wins.need: Long service life when it is cycled every day
wins.claim: BLUETTI rates the mini for 6,000+ cycles. The rivals' own makers rate the Elite 100 V2 for 4,000+ cycles to 80% and the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 for 4,000 cycles to at least 80%. These are maker ratings, not measurements.

wins.need: Getting close to the rated capacity in real use
wins.claim: The YouTube reviewer There's A Trick For That got 903 Wh out of the rated 1,004 Wh (about 90%), as reported by The Cool Down. OutdoorGearLab (Kenji Mowrey) measured the Elite 100 V2 at 890 Wh of 1,024 Wh (87%). The two figures come from different testers using different methods, so they suggest a difference but do not prove one.
wins.who: There's A Trick For That (reported by Vivian Tran, The Cool Down, 2026-09-06); OutdoorGearLab, 2026-07-23

wins.need: Keeping a PC, router or CPAP running through a blackout
wins.claim: The Solar Lab measured 97% efficiency and says that is far above the 80 to 85% of some units it has tested. In There's A Trick For That's test, a workstation drawing about 600 W stayed on when wall power was cut. BLUETTI rates the switchover at 10 ms. That 10 ms equals the Elite 100 V2 and Anker C1000 Gen 2, so it is not an advantage over them.
wins.figure: 97% efficiency (The Solar Lab); a 600 W PC load stayed up through the cut; 10 ms switchover (BLUETTI)
wins.who: The Solar Lab; There's A Trick For That via The Cool Down

weak.claim: Low continuous output. BLUETTI says total AC output must not exceed 700 W. In There's A Trick For That's load checks the unit shut down at 900 W. The Elite 100 V2 is rated 1,800 W, the DELTA 3 Classic 1,800 W and the Anker C1000 Gen 2 2,000 W.
weak.figure: 700 W rated; shut down at 900 W

weak.claim: Limited solar input. The Solar Lab calls it 'a little low'. The Elite 100 V2 takes 1,000 W of solar and the Anker C1000 Gen 2 takes 600 W.
Capacity cannot be expanded (The Solar Lab). The EcoFlow DELTA 3 ($579) expands to 1 to 5 kWh.
Uses a lot of power doing nothing. The Solar Lab measured about 13.5 W with the AC inverter on and nothing plugged in, which it estimates would empty the battery in about three days.
weak.figure: About 13.5 W idle with AC on

weak.claim: Slower to recharge from the wall than its rivals. BLUETTI says about 90 minutes to 80%. BLUETTI says 45 minutes to 80% for the Elite 100 V2, and Anker says 49 minutes to 100% for the C1000 Gen 2. The Solar Lab measured about two hours from empty to full on the mini.
weak.figure: About 90 min to 80% (BLUETTI); about 2 h to full (The Solar Lab)

weak.claim: Possibly louder than the Elite 100 V2. Dan Miller of BackupPowerHub, citing BLUETTI's specs, lists a 50 dB maximum. BLUETTI's own V2 page says 30 dB under 600 W. Neither figure is a measurement.
weak.figure: 50 dB max (spec quoted by BackupPowerHub); Elite 100 V2: 30 dB

wins_for: People who want about 1 kWh in the smallest box: apartments, under a desk, car trunks
Blackout backup for low-draw devices: router, laptops, a PC drawing about 600 W or less, a CPAP. CGMagazine (Marcus Kenneth) ran a heated-humidifier CPAP from bedtime to sunrise
Buyers on a budget who want the lowest price per Wh at a maker store ($429)
Weekend car camping with one 100 to 200 W panel, which stays under the 350 W solar limit (arithmetic)
not_for: Microwaves, coffee makers, kettles or anything over 700 W continuous: get the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 ($499, 1,800 W) or the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic ($459, 1,800 W)
Charging mainly from big solar arrays: the Elite 100 V2 takes 1,000 W of solar against the mini's 350 W
Shoppers who may want more capacity later: the EcoFlow DELTA 3 ($579) expands to 5 kWh
Whole-house or full-size-fridge backup over several days: 903 Wh measured is far too little; look at home backup systems
Fast top-ups between outages: the Anker C1000 Gen 2 charges to 100% in 49 minutes (Anker) and the Elite 100 V2 reaches 80% in 45 minutes (BLUETTI)

rivals.price: $499.00, in stock, BLUETTI US store, https://www.bluettipower.com/products/elite-100-v2-portable-power-station, read 2026-11-15
rivals.where_it_beats_ours: 1,800 W output with 2,700 W lifting, against 700 W; 1,000 W solar against 350 W; 80% in 45 minutes on AC; 30 dB claimed under 600 W. It is $70 more, has a 107 sq in footprint and weighs 25 lb.
1,800 W output with 3,600 W surge; 0 to 80% in 45 minutes on AC; up to 5-year warranty if registered in the EcoFlow app (EcoFlow store listing). Only $30 more.

rivals.model: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 (1,024 Wh, 2,000 W)
rivals.where_it_beats_ours: 2,000 W output with 3,000 W peak; 600 W solar; 49 minutes to 100% at 1,600 W (Anker). It is larger (124 sq in) and heavier (24.9 lb).

rivals.price: $549.00, black listed as sold out, https://www.jackery.com/products/jackery-homepower-1000-v2 (storecheck search), read 2026-11-15
rivals.where_it_beats_ours: 1,500 W output; Jackery claims a full charge in 50 minutes and under 30 dB. It is $120 more.

targets.headline: Which BLUETTI power station should you buy: the small 1 kWh one or the high-output one?
targets.why_it_wins_there: It is BLUETTI's cheapest 1 kWh unit ($429 against $499 for the Elite 100 V2, BLUETTI store, 2026-11-15) with a 26% smaller footprint (arithmetic from BLUETTI's dimensions). A reviewer measured 903 Wh usable (The Cool Down). The page should be honest that the Elite 100 V2 wins for anything over 700 W.

targets.search: best portable power station for home backup
targets.headline: The best small power station for keeping Wi-Fi, a CPAP and laptops on in an outage
targets.why_it_wins_there: 903 Wh measured (There's A Trick For That via The Cool Down). A 600 W PC stayed up when wall power was cut. 10 ms switchover (BLUETTI). Lowest $/Wh of the stations priced today. Recommend it only for essentials, not kitchen appliances.

targets.search: home battery backup for power outages
targets.headline: A shelf-sized battery for power outages: what it runs and what it can't
targets.why_it_wins_there: For low-draw loads it gives the most stored energy per dollar and the smallest footprint. It runs a router or CPAP all night (CGMagazine CPAP night; BLUETTI rates a Wi-Fi router at 39.2 h). The page must state the 700 W limit and the 900 W shutdown.

targets.headline: A compact 1 kWh solar generator for car camping that won't fill your trunk
targets.why_it_wins_there: 79 sq in footprint and 23.6 lb (BLUETTI). BLUETTI sells it with a 200 W panel for $649, and that panel stays under the 350 W solar limit (arithmetic). The Solar Lab calls the 350 W limit 'a little low', so mention it.

targets.headline: 1 kWh power stations compared: which ones actually run 1,000-watt appliances?
targets.why_it_wins_there: It only wins for shoppers who mean 1,000 Wh of capacity: lowest $/Wh and smallest footprint. For a 1,000 W load it loses (700 W rated, shut down at 900 W per The Cool Down), so feature it as the capacity-for-the-money pick, not the output pick.

record.name: BLUETTI Elite 100 mini Portable Power Station, 1,004.8 Wh, 700 W
specs: 9 total: 3 AC, 6 DC; USB-C 140 W + 65 W
record.warranty: BLUETTI's US warranty policy says 'For the product of portable power station, the warranty period varies from 24 months to 72 months' and does not list this model's period. Coverage is limited to the country of purchase and excludes unauthorized resellers (https://www.bluettipower.com/pages/warranty-policy, read 2026-11-15).
record.returns: 30 days from purchase. Items must be complete and unused in original packaging, and BLUETTI may refuse used items. The buyer pays return shipping, which is deducted from the refund when BLUETTI issues the RMA. Refund within 14 business days after the item reaches BLUETTI's warehouse (https://www.bluettipower.com/policies/refund-policy, read 2026-11-15).
record.summary: A 1 kWh LFP power station with a 9.3 x 8.5 in footprint and a 700 W inverter. A reviewer measured 903 Wh usable (There's A Trick For That via The Cool Down), and at $429 it has the lowest price per Wh of the 1 kWh units we priced.
record.fit: Compact backup for routers, laptops, PCs and CPAPs, and light car camping. Not for kitchen appliances or anything drawing over 700 W.
caveats: Rated 700 W total. In There's A Trick For That's test it shut down at 900 W (The Cool Down).
Solar input tops out at 350 W (BLUETTI); The Solar Lab calls it 'a little low'.
Capacity cannot be expanded (The Solar Lab).
Draws about 13.5 W idle with the AC inverter on (The Solar Lab).
Recharging takes about 90 min to 80% (BLUETTI), slower than 1,800 to 2,000 W rivals.

unsourced: Elite 100 mini user manual: BLUETTI support PDFs downloaded but could not be read in this environment. Surge (1,050 W for 2 s), solar voltage (12 to 60 V, 10 A), 50 dB noise, operating and charging temperatures and Power Lifting 1,400 W were seen only in BackupPowerHub's spec-based review (and Power Lifting in the iTWire launch article, not re-opened), so they are left out of the record specs.
Model-specific warranty length: BLUETTI's US warranty pages give only 24 to 72 months for power stations. BackupPowerHub says 3 years, but no BLUETTI page confirming that was found.
